headline: Parliament Passes Nationwide Lifejacket Rule as Grocery Prices and Benefit Errors Fuel Debate
summary: Parliament passed a requirement for people aboard recreational craft up to six metres long to wear lifejackets while underway, with supporters saying the change could prevent deaths. Question time and a lengthy election-year debate also focused on supermarket competition, wrongly suspended benefit payments, jobs and the cost of living, while MPs advanced health, housing, energy and Treaty-settlement measures.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Rejects Price-Gouging Ban as Supermarket Competition Comes Under Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Grocery prices affect household budgets, and the debate focused on whether current reforms will deliver more competition and lower costs for shoppers.
topicSummaries.content: Green co-leader Marama Davidson challenged Economic Growth Minister Nicola Willis over grocery prices and the market share held by Foodstuffs and Woolworths. Willis cited the Commerce Commission’s finding that prices remained above the OECD average and the two major supermarket groups held 82 percent of the market, saying the Government was working to lower barriers to new competitors and strengthen competition rules. She rejected a proposed price-gouging ban as unworkable, while pointing to easing food-price inflation; Davidson questioned when shoppers would see results from the reforms.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Marama Davidson (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does she accept the Commerce Commission’s findings that the supermarket duopoly has been making over $1 million a day in excess profits, and is that fair on regular people struggling to put food on the table?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, I support the Commerce Commission’s findings but not necessarily the way that they are paraphrased by Green Party members.

topicSummaries.topic: Minister Orders Review After Benefit Payments Were Wrongly Suspended
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: People whose benefits are stopped unexpectedly may struggle to cover essentials such as food, rent and transport.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime pressed Social Development and Employment Minister Louise Upston about payments wrongly suspended after the Social Security (Mandatory Reviews) Amendment Act 2025 took effect. Upston said the suspensions were unacceptable, that the Ministry of Social Development had been directed to reinstate affected payments, and that she expected a review identifying how many people were affected and what further steps were needed by 10 September. She did not provide a figure in the House, and Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick asked whether compensation would be considered; the Minister did not directly address that part of the question.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How many beneficiaries have had their benefit payments wrongly suspended since the law change?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: As I said in the House yesterday, I don’t have that number; that is what I’m expecting to get from the review on 10 September.

topicSummaries.topic: Auckland Unemployment and Hospital Staffing Put Under Pressure in Question Time
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Employment levels and access to nurses affect household security and the availability of local health services.
topicSummaries.content: Labour Deputy Leader Carmel Sepuloni questioned Auckland Minister Simon Watts about unemployment and reported reductions in nursing positions at Auckland City and Middlemore hospitals. Sepuloni cited more than 30,000 Aucklanders having lost jobs over three years and a 39 percent rise in Jobseeker Support Work Ready recipients. Watts acknowledged unemployment remained higher than desired, blamed inherited economic conditions and said the Government’s Auckland deal and infrastructure investment would support jobs and growth; he also defended the Government’s record on health services.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is Auckland going backwards when there has a been a 39 percent increase in the number of Jobseeker Support Work Ready recipients in Auckland in just the last three years?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It is fair to note that Auckland’s unemployment levels aren’t where we want them to be. However, it is fair to also indicate that when we came in, there was an economy in recession.

topicSummaries.topic: Election-Year Tax Debate Centres on Capital Gains Tax and Small Businesses
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The parties’ competing tax proposals could affect business owners, investors and the revenue available for public services.
topicSummaries.content: The general debate was dominated by competing claims over tax policy. National ministers argued Labour’s proposed 28 percent capital gains tax on commercial property would also affect small businesses that own their premises, while Labour disputed National’s broader list of possible taxes and said the Government was planning further public-service cuts. ACT, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and NZ First also set out differing positions on tax, spending and economic policy. The exchanges formed part of a wider election campaign argument about how to fund public services and support growth.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This is an issue where the contrast couldn’t be clearer. National truly wants to reward aspiration and effort to back businesses to invest, grow, and get ahead.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: National cuts; Labour invests.

topicSummaries.topic: Reserve Bank Raises Official Cash Rate to 2.75 Percent as Inflation Concerns Persist
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Interest-rate changes can influence borrowing costs, while fuel-driven inflation can raise household and business expenses.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis reported that the Reserve Bank had raised the official cash rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent, following an earlier increase in July. Willis said the move was widely expected and that fixed-term mortgage rates should see little or no change as a result. She attributed the decision to the Reserve Bank’s inflation mandate, higher fuel prices and a strengthening economy, and said restrained government spending was limiting inflationary pressure. In a separate exchange, Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick argued that government energy policy had left New Zealand exposed to imported fossil-fuel inflation; Willis rejected that claim and defended investment in energy security and renewables.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Can the Minister confirm that her Government came to office and cut active investment in decarbonising industry while also committing hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayer funds to subsidise fossil fuels, resulting in our economy having greater exposure to imported fossil fuel inflation?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, in terms of things that have exposed us to imported fossil fuel inflation, the fateful decision to ban oil and gas exploration has exposed us to Indonesian coal prices more than any other decision.

topicSummaries.topic: Parliament Passes Lifejacket Requirement for Recreational Boats up to Six Metres
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The rule is intended to reduce preventable drownings by requiring people to wear lifejackets rather than merely carry them aboard.
topicSummaries.content: MPs passed the Maritime Transport (Lifejackets on Recreational Craft) Amendment Bill at its final reading. The bill requires everyone on a recreational craft up to six metres long to wear an appropriately sized lifejacket while the craft is underway, replacing a narrower proposal focused on people under 15 and establishing a consistent national rule. Supporters cited evidence that most recreational boating deaths involved people not wearing lifejackets and estimated the change could save about 10 lives a year. The Associate Minister of Transport said Maritime New Zealand would lead an education-first campaign, with an infringement regime expected to be developed for 2027.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Shane Reti (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill is looking to save an average of 10 lives per year, with a 60 percent reduction in small recreational craft drownings through wearing life jackets—not just carrying them, not at skipper discretion, and not varied across regional councils.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Tangi Utikere (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This is a bill that, while it has taken some time to work through the Parliament, I think is a good move, because we’ve got it into a position where it is effectively going to save lives.

topicSummaries.topic: Free Cervical Screening for Eligible Women Set to Begin in March 2027
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Removing appointment costs is intended to make a potentially life-saving screening service accessible to more women.
topicSummaries.content: Women’s Minister Nicola Grigg told the House that cervical screening would be free for all eligible women aged 25 to 69 from 1 March 2027. She said almost 800,000 more women would be eligible for free screening and that cost currently prevents some women from attending. The Government also launched a plan aimed at eliminating cervical cancer in New Zealand by 2040, with measures focused on HPV vaccination, screening, follow-up care and timely treatment.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dr Vanessa Weenink (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Why is making cervical screening free so important?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Grigg (National)
keyExchanges.quote: But screening only works if women can access it, and we know that cost can be a barrier for some women.

topicSummaries.topic: Ōtautahi Community Housing Trust Bill Passes to Expand Its Reach
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The change allows an established community housing provider to work beyond Christchurch and Banks Peninsula, potentially supporting housing provision elsewhere in the South Island.
topicSummaries.content: The House passed the Ōtautahi Community Housing Trust (Trust Variation) Bill, a private bill sponsored by Labour MP Megan Woods and supported across parties. It amends the trust’s deed so it can operate outside Christchurch and Banks Peninsula, responding to requests from Canterbury mayors for the provider to work across a wider area. Woods said the trust could bring its experience in social and affordable rentals and shared-equity housing to other communities, while the bill retains Christchurch and Banks Peninsula as its primary focus. The bill passed without amendment.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: It is with pride as a Cantabrian that I stand here with this bill that means we can expand what has been happening in Christchurch further beyond our city limits and that we can see Greater Christchurch and the Waimakariri and Selwyn and beyond benefit from some of the innovative approaches that ŌCHT has taken over time.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Grigg (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We’re very, very pleased to support the Ōtautahi Community Housing Trust (Trust Variation) Bill at the third reading.

topicSummaries.topic: Trust Horizon Gains Wider Charitable Grant-Making Powers
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The change allows a community trust in the Eastern Bay of Plenty to support a broader range of local needs beyond energy-related projects.
topicSummaries.content: Parliament passed the Trust Horizon (Trust Variation) Bill, broadening the charitable purposes for which the trust can provide support while retaining energy projects as an eligible focus. The trust holds assets valued at more than $200 million, and the sponsor’s representative said its existing deed limited the projects it could fund. Labour supported the bill but questioned whether energy investment needs had been exhausted and how the expanded grant-making would reflect local priorities. The bill passed without amendment after MPs noted that 80.7 percent of respondents to a local poll supported the change.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: What evidence is there that the trust has exhausted all its energy-related opportunities for expenditure?

keyExchanges.speaker: Tom Rutherford (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I’m advised that there are not enough applications lodged, plus the trust goes out proactively to their community and they have expended all available income where they can, hence why they are seeking to broaden their remit.

topicSummaries.topic: Parliament Passes Two Whanganui and Waikaremoana Claims Settlements
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The settlements formally recognise Crown breaches of Te Tiriti, provide redress and set out commitments intended to support iwi and hapū aspirations.
topicSummaries.content: During the extended sitting, Parliament passed the Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui Claims Settlement Bill and the Ngāti Ruapani mai Waikaremoana Claims Settlement Bill. Treaty Negotiations Minister Paul Goldsmith said the Whanganui settlement included the return of 27 culturally significant sites, a $15.5 million cultural revitalisation fund and $30 million in relationship, financial and commercial redress, as well as rights to purchase commercial properties. The Ngāti Ruapani settlement provides $24 million in financial and commercial redress, the return of cultural properties and about 12,000 hectares of land being added to Te Urewera, to be cared for in common with Tūhoe. MPs from across parties acknowledged the settlements could not fully compensate for historical harms and emphasised that the Crown must honour its commitments after legislation passes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Of course, as all Ministers say, this settlement can never fully compensate Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui for what they have suffered because of Crown actions.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: A settlement should not be regarded at all as the end of a relationship; it should be just the beginning of a brand new chapter.

conclusion: Parliament delivered cross-party support for life-safety and settlement legislation, while the unresolved pressure points remained the cost of living, access to support and services, and the competing economic priorities of an election campaign.
